question: Is Salat al-Shukr (Shukrana Namaz) a bid'ah, and does the prostration of thanks require wudu?
asked: Can you tell us the rulings regarding Salat al-Shukr, or Shukrana Namaz? Somebody told me that it is bid'ah to do Salat al-Shukr.
answer:
Firstly, it is definitely and authentically reported from the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ that anytime some good news came to him, he would prostrate immediately. And this is something that is reported in many narrations, of them the famous hadith of Abu Bakr radiAllahu anhu, reported in all of the books of the Sunan, that whenever good news came to the Prophet ﷺ, whenever he was told about any bushra, kharra sajidan shakiran lillahi 'azza wa jall: he would fall down in sajda as a matter of thanks to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, one of the Sahabah said: I was there when the Prophet ﷺ was informed that a certain expedition he had sent was victorious over the enemy. He was in the house of Aisha radiAllahu anha, and he stood up, meaning he entered the masjid, and he fell down in sajda. So there is definitely something called sajdat al-shukr.

And we also know this from the hadith of Abdul Rahman ibn Awf radiAllahu anhu. Abdul Rahman said: one day I went out with the Prophet ﷺ to a certain land outside of Madinah, and as we were walking, he just took a turn and faced the qibla and fell down in sajda, and stayed there for a long time. So they're literally on the road, and he just falls into sajda. Then the Prophet ﷺ said to Abdul Rahman ibn Awf when he stood up: "Jibreel just came to me now, and he told me that Allah has said to him to tell him that whoever gives salat upon the Prophet, Allah will give salat upon him; whoever gives salam to the Prophet, Allah will give salam to him. So I fell down in sajda, shukran lillah."

So all of these tell us that whenever good news comes to us, we should fall down in sajda. Sadly, this is something we have not done; we don't do this anymore. We need to revive the Sunnah. Anytime you hear any good news: you are blessed with a rizq, you are blessed with a child, you found out that some relative of yours or child of yours is cured of something, any good news, you should fall down immediately in sajda.

And Ka'b ibn Malik, of the famous three people who were held up in Tabuk (remember the famous story that Allah revealed in the Qur'an), the famous narration goes that when Ka'b ibn Malik heard the verses from Surah Tawbah, he said, "I fell down in sajda." First thing he did, in his own house, even before he came back to the Prophet, he fell down in sajda.

So all of this is authentically reported. Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, when he heard of the death of Musaylama the liar in the wars of the Riddah, and he was in the masjid of the Prophet, when the person came and said, "We won, Musaylama is dead," in front of everybody he fell down in sajda. And Ali ibn Abi Talib, in the famous battle with the Khawarij, when he killed Dhul-Thudayya, the famous incident, he also fell down in sajda. In between the corpses, he fell down in sajda.

Now, we are talking about the sajda of shukr right now. There is an ikhtilaf about the sajda of shukr: must you meet all of the conditions of salah when you fall into sajda? I.e., what are the conditions of salah? Number one, wudu. Number two, face the qibla. Number three, takbirat al-ihram. Good, number four? What else are you going to do? Satr al-'awra, right. What if you're in your pajama shorts and the phone call comes that, oh, your relative has been cured, whatnot? Okay, what should you do in that state?

So the default position of most of the ulama (listen to this): sajdat al-shukr is a partial salah, so it takes the rulings of salah. So the majority would say that you should stand up, go do wudu, face the qibla, make sure your 'awra is covered, say Allahu akbar, fall down in sajda, then get up and say salam. Is that clear? This is the default position of the majority of the ummah, and it is a very good position.

Counter to this, we have many of the ulama, including al-Tabari, Ibn Hazm, Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Shawkani, al-San'ani. And all of these, if you know anything about them, they're all kind of sort of the independent guys; they're the people that are thinking outside of the box, typically, all of them. They said no, sajdat al-shukr is not salah. In all of these narrations, and we have like a dozen of them or whatever, never is it narrated that the Prophet ﷺ or the Sahabah did what? Stand up and go do wudu, or do anything else. Right then and there, without even takbir, they just fell down in sajda. If you say Allahu akbar as you're going down, no problem. But to say Allahu akbar, and then go down, and then "salamu alaykum", they would say: where's the evidence for this? There's no evidence.

In fact, their argument, Ibn Taymiyyah and others, they say the purpose of sajdat al-shukr is to thank Allah fil-hal, meaning right then and there, when your emotions are bursting up. At that point you humble yourself in front of Allah: "Alhamdulillah, Allah blessed me with this." For you to calm down, "Wait, I don't have wudu, let me wait," what's going to happen? That emotion will be gone.

So the counter argument is that there is no evidence that sajdat al-shukr needs any requirements, even wudu, because it's not salah. Just like you can say subhanAllah without wudu, you can say Allahu akbar without wudu, you can say Subhana Rabbiyal A'la without wudu. You can do many things. You can read the Qur'an without wudu by ijma'; you can recite Fatiha and any surah sitting here without wudu. So why can't you just do sajda? Because it's not salah; it does not take the ruling of salah.

And no doubt, I personally sympathize with this position. Whoever wishes to follow the madhahib in this regard, because the default, really, of all four is that they do say that sajda takes the ruling of salah, that's good, no problem. But the counter argument is very weighty, and there are great ulama that have said this. This is sajdat al-shukr.

I went into a tangent for our benefit. The question was not about sajdat al-shukr; it was about Shukrana Namaz, the Salat al-Shukr. Now, the reason why this brother asked (I didn't mention the whole thing), he basically said, "Somebody told me that it is bid'ah to do Salat al-Shukr." And this is obviously... I have to be gentle here; I don't want to be too harsh. But there's no doubt we've seen in the last 20 years or so a trend that really has been very, very harsh on generic good deeds, and they've said things like sajdat al-shukr or salat al-shukr becomes a bid'ah. Why, they say? Because the Prophet ﷺ did not command us to pray two raka'at.

So the difference, of course, between sajdat al-shukr and salat al-shukr is what? Sajda is you just go up and down. And salah means you will pray two raka'at: you will do wudu, face the qibla, cover your 'awra, you will pray two raka'at properly as a matter of thanks to Allah for something good that has happened.

So one group of ulama, modern (primarily, almost all of them are modern), they say this is a bid'ah, you should not do it, and it is something that is wrong to do. And we respond in two ways. Firstly, by saying that even if there is no explicit evidence for two raka'at after a specific blessing, the general texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah tell us that when something good happens, we thank Allah in any way: whether it is through dhikr, whether it is through Qur'an, whether it is through sadaqah, whether it is through sawm, or whether it is through salah. So we flip it around: the generalities of the Qur'an and Sunnah are enough for us to say that it is completely permissible to pray two raka'at if you get good news.

Now, somebody says, "But the Prophet ﷺ did not specifically tell us to do that." And we respond to this by saying that this is a more technical issue: what defines bid'ah, and what defines something going against the Sunnah. It is true, if somebody were to say that it is Sunnah to pray two raka'at, we will say, what is your evidence? But to say it is bid'ah to pray two raka'at, that also, we say, what is your evidence? The general texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah say: when something good happens, you thank Allah.

And if somebody feels like fasting: say good news, he got a very good score, and he says, "You know what, I'm going to fast tomorrow, alhamdulillah." Somebody's going to say that's wrong? Somebody got good news and says, "I'm going to give five hundred dollars sadaqah for the yatama." Are we going to say, "Astaghfirullah, don't give, because the Prophet ﷺ did not say give $500 to the yateem when good news happens"? There is a level of common sense that we have to be cognizant of. So generally speaking, any good deed in response to good news is a good deed. No problem.

However, interestingly enough, specifically when it comes to Salat al-Shukr, we do have narrations about this, but there is some controversy over their authenticity. It is reported in the Sunan of Ibn Majah. Ibn Majah is one of the six books, as you know; true, it is the last of the six, but it is one of the six books. And Ibn Majah has a title in his book, in Kitab al-Salah, the chapter regarding Salat al-Shukr and Sajdat al-Shukr. That is a title in his book. Then he brings forth a narration by Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa that when the Prophet ﷺ was told of the death of Abu Jahl (Abu Jahl died around the Battle of Badr), the Prophet ﷺ, when he was told of the death of Abu Jahl, prayed two raka'at to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Okay, this hadith is reported where? Ibn Majah. Very good, Ibn Majah.

Now, the only issue: one person in this chain, he is not known. Nobody knows anything about him. He's the narrator from the Tabi'i, and he's just a person; we know his name, we don't know anything about him. And some ulama, Ibn Hajar included, found other narrations, and they said this hadith is hasan, authentic. And other ulama, including the modern al-Albani, said this hadith is slightly weak. Not very weak; slightly weak, just a little bit weak.

The point, though, is that even if the hadith is slightly weak: number one, Ibn Majah believes this to be Salat al-Shukr, and he quotes from it, and he has the title. Number two, the generalities of the Qur'an and Sunnah tell us when a good deed happens, you do a good deed in return.

And in fact, this is something that we find in other scholars as well. Of them is the famous scholar of the Salaf themselves, one of the great scholars of the Salaf, Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi. Al-Marwazi said: as for salah and sajda when a blessing comes from Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, then this is Sunnah. And of the evidences for this, he says (this is al-Marwazi; al-Marwazi died in the 3rd century, a very long time ago), of the evidences: when Allah blessed the Prophet ﷺ with the conquest of Makkah, he did ghusl and he prayed eight raka'at, shukran lillah.

Now, this is a famous narration in Bukhari and Muslim, that when the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah, he prayed eight raka'at. Okay, this is well known. Al-Marwazi says this is Salat al-Shukr. Eight: like he did it a lot, very thankful to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And Ibn Hajar, the famous scholar of hadith, he says in these eight raka'at is the evidence for Salat al-Shukr. This is what Ibn Hajar says.

So the concept of praying two raka'at, or four raka'at, or ten raka'at, or twenty raka'at, just to pray to Allah when good news happens, what's wrong with that? It's good. Go ahead and pray. Why would you want to stop somebody from praying when a good deed happens to them? Right, and again, this is why sometimes these people, we know their zealousness is positive, because they want to protect the Sunnah, but sometimes in your zealousness you lose track of reality. What is wrong with a Muslim man or woman praying two raka'at to Allah? They're not saying this is something wajib; nobody says it's wajib. But what's wrong when a good deed happens? What's the big deal?

We have great ulama, al-Marwazi, Ibn Hajar and others. And in fact, even Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim (ironically, this group looks up to them so much, but they rarely read their books in detail). Ibn Taymiyyah says that the scholars recommended that generals, when they conquer villages, they too should pray eight raka'at, like the Prophet ﷺ prayed eight raka'at, as a shukr to Allah. Now, this is not quite Salat al-Shukr for anything, but the concept Ibn Taymiyyah is saying: when a magnificent good thing happens, like the conquest of a city, then the people who are responsible, the general and whatnot, should pray shukr to Allah, eight raka'at. Ibn al-Qayyim as well has the same thing. He called it Salat al-Fath, the salat of victory: that you should pray eight raka'at when a victory happens. And the concept is over there.

So inshaAllah, with this we say: **it is Sunnah to do sajdat al-shukr; there is no question about it. As for Salat al-Shukr, the least that can be said, it is not bid'ah.** And if somebody wants to pray, alhamdulillah. And if somebody believes the hadith to be not authentic, well, then do something else. Give some sadaqah and charity; no problem with that.
